title: Files that last
summary: Saving and AutoSave, file types (.xlsx, .xlsm, .csv), and how Excel versions differ.
objectives: Save, and Save As with a new name, place or file type.
Know what AutoSave and version history do, and what changes between Excel versions.

p: **Save** keeps one file up to date. **Save As** makes a new copy.
The first time you save, Excel asks for a name and a folder.
Make it a habit: Ctrl+S every few minutes.
In real life: Opens March's file and uses Save As to make *Accounts April.xlsx*, so March stays exactly as it was.

p: On OneDrive or SharePoint, every change saves itself, and you can go back to an earlier copy.
File › Info › **Version History** brings back an older copy.
On your own laptop AutoSave is off, so press Ctrl+S.
AutoRecover helps after a crash, but don't rely on it.
In real life: Shares one budget on OneDrive. When someone overwrote a total, they restored yesterday's version in a minute.

check.q: Your file is saved on your laptop's desktop. What keeps your latest changes?
check.explain: AutoSave only works for files on OneDrive or SharePoint. On your own laptop, **Ctrl+S**.

why.2: Closing asks whether to save; it doesn't save for you.
why.3: Only AutoRecover runs, and only for crashes.

p: The letters after the dot decide what a file can hold.
Use **.xlsx** for almost everything.
CSV is how systems swap data; PDF is for sending a final copy.

plain text: one sheet, values only

slides.h: Why saving as CSV loses things
p: CSV keeps only plain values. Colours, formulas and extra sheets disappear.
Excel warns about **possible data loss**: choose Save As › Excel Workbook (.xlsx).
Downloaded a CSV? Save it as .xlsx before you start working.
In real life: Downloaded a bank statement as CSV, added formulas, saved, and lost them all. Now he saves as .xlsx first.

p: Files open across versions, but brand-new functions can show as errors on older ones.
Sharing a file? Ask which Excel the other person uses.
Excel for the web handles most everyday work.
In real life: Its lab runs an older Excel, so students avoid the newest functions in files they share with teachers.

check.q: You open a CSV, add formulas and colours, and save it as CSV. What happens?
check.explain: CSV is plain text: formulas, formats and extra sheets are lost. Save as **.xlsx** to keep them.

why.0: CSV can't store formatting or formulas.
why.2: It saves, just without the extras.
why.3: Excel asks, but keeps CSV if you say so.

demo.intro: Save a copy of the workbook as an Excel Workbook with a new name.

frames.say: Press **F12** (or File › Save As). Choose where to save: a folder on your laptop or OneDrive.
Type a clear file name, then open **Save as type** and pick **Excel Workbook (*.xlsx)**.
Back in the window, the new name shows in the title bar. On OneDrive, switch **AutoSave** on.

lab.intro: Decide on file types, then put the Save As steps in order. Finish with a real save in Excel.

tasks.prompt: A bank lets you download your statement as CSV. You add a formula and some colour, then press Ctrl+S, keeping CSV. What happens?
hints: Think about what CSV can store.
CSV is plain text: values and commas.
Formulas and colours can’t be stored in plain text.
tasks.explain: Save As › Excel Workbook (.xlsx) to keep your work.
options: The formula is replaced by its value and the colours are lost

tasks.prompt: Which file type do you need for a workbook with macros?
hints: Most types refuse to hold code for safety.

tasks.prompt: You must share a final fee summary that nobody should change by accident and that looks the same on every phone. Best format?
hints: Layout must stay the same everywhere.
tasks.explain: File › Export › PDF, or choose PDF in Save As.

tasks.prompt: Put the steps for saving a copy as an Excel Workbook in order.
hints: Then choose where, then the name.
The file type comes just before Save.
items: Choose Excel Workbook (*.xlsx) as the type

tasks.prompt: Your file is on OneDrive with AutoSave on. You made a mess an hour ago. What helps?
hints: AutoSave keeps saving, so Undo may not reach that far.
tasks.explain: Version History lists earlier saves; open one and restore it.

real.title: Save a workbook properly
steps: Add a new sheet with the ⊕ button and rename it **Summary**.
Press F12 (Save As) and save it as **Excel Workbook (.xlsx)** with a new name, like *Shop orders - your name.xlsx*.

checks.label: Your name is in Summary!A1
checks.msg: Type your name in A1 of the Summary sheet.

checks.label: The original sheets are still there

quiz.q: What does Ctrl+S do the first time you save a new workbook?
options: Asks where to save it and what to call it
quiz.explain: The first save is really a Save As.

quiz.q: Which file type keeps only one sheet of plain values?
quiz.explain: CSV is plain text: no formats, no formulas, one sheet.

quiz.q: Excel warns “Some features might be lost if you save this workbook in CSV”. What should you usually do?
options: Save As an Excel Workbook (.xlsx) instead
quiz.explain: Unless a system needs CSV, keep your work in .xlsx.

quiz.q: A colleague on Excel 2016 opens your file and sees errors where you used a brand-new function. Why?
options: Older versions don’t have the newest functions
quiz.explain: New functions arrive in Microsoft 365 first.

quiz.q: Which is free to use in a browser?
quiz.explain: Excel for the web is free with a Microsoft account.

points: **Ctrl+S** saves; **F12 / Save As** makes a copy with a new name, place or type.
**.xlsx** keeps everything; **.csv** keeps one sheet of values; **.xlsm** holds macros; **.pdf** is a read-only picture.
On OneDrive, **AutoSave** and **Version History** protect your work.
recap.cheat: Work in .xlsx. Export to .csv or .pdf only when someone needs that format.

cards.back: Formulas (replaced by values), formatting, and every sheet but one.
